blocks.content: A Pod stuck in the Pending phase, covered in the Pod Phases topic, means one of two things: it has not been scheduled yet, or it has been scheduled but its containers have not started, the most common real cause by far is the first.

As covered in the Pod Phases topic, Pending covers both "not scheduled to a node at all" and "scheduled, but containers still starting," these are genuinely different situations that happen to share the same reported phase.

blocks.alt: Two different real situations, both reported under the same phase name

blocks.content: In practice, a Pod stuck Pending for any real length of time is almost always a scheduling failure, the scheduler simply could not find a node it was willing to place the Pod on, covered in full in the next topic.

blocks.alt: A scheduling failure, by far the most common real-world cause of a stuck Pod

blocks.content: Exactly as covered in the Observability module's Debugging Pods topic, kubectl describe pod is the first move, its Events section names the specific, real reason a Pod has not been scheduled or started.

blocks.alt: The Events section, naming the specific, real reason directly

blocks.content:
kubectl describe pod my-app
# Events:
#   Warning  FailedScheduling  2m  default-scheduler  0/3 nodes available: insufficient memory

code.content:
kubectl describe pod my-app
# Events:
#   Warning  FailedScheduling  2m  default-scheduler  0/3 nodes available: insufficient memory

codes.bash:
kubectl describe pod my-app
# Events:
#   Warning  FailedScheduling  2m  default-scheduler  0/3 nodes available: insufficient memory

blocks.content: The most frequent real causes are insufficient cluster-wide resources, no node matching a required nodeSelector or affinity rule (covered in the Scheduling module), or an unbound PVC (covered in the Storage module) the Pod depends on.

blocks.alt: A handful of recurring causes, each pointing at a different earlier module

blocks.content: Exactly the systematic debugging order covered in the Observability module, describe first, then logs if it did get far enough to start, then exec if genuinely still needed, applies here as well.

blocks.alt: The same systematic order covered in the Observability module, applied to this specific symptom

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A Pod stuck Pending is most often a scheduling failure, kubectl describe pod's Events section names the specific reason directly, almost always the fastest path to an answer.
Insufficient resources, unmatched affinity rules, and unbound PVCs are the most common recurring causes, each traceable back to an earlier module in this course.
